source_locator.description: Palace play opening; Kesari Varman speaks from behind the curtain, but the following source lines have an empty printed speaker field.

translation.english_text: (A play in the palace. Kesari Varman speaks from behind the curtain.)
notes: The direction establishes the dramatic situation; the following empty-speaker lines remain unlabelled metadata.

source_locator.description: Opening prologue printed with empty speaker fields after the behind-curtain direction.

translation.english_text: What you are about to see is no tale of fancy, but a picture for thought: the history of an empire ruined by a beauty! King Uthama Purushan was a grove of classical Tamil. The breeze that bathed his mind was Kamalavathi, the crowned queen! The Pandiyan killed the queen's father. Bearing heart-shaking news came a court painter, Eeswari Varman! His wife Devasena was a Chitrangi. She came like a breeze. She turned into a storm. The moment that smiling storm entered...
notes: No speaker label is invented even though the preceding direction identifies Kesari Varman behind the curtain.
The grove/breeze/storm image chain and `செந்தமிழ்` register are preserved rather than summarized.

source_locator.description: The play begins after the unlabelled prologue.

translation.english_text: (The play begins.)
Appa!... Appa...!
Do not cry, Kamala, do not cry!
Did Father-in-law say anything in his final hours?...
notes: The exact source label `வர்மா` remains unresolved in character metadata and is not normalized here.

translation.english_text: There is, Prabhu...

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker quoted message and report following Eeswari Varman's labelled `இருக்கிறது ப்ரபூ...`; spans PDF 13→14.

translation.english_text: ‘My grandson Ajayan himself must avenge the Pandiyan. Recovering my Navaratna throne is his responsibility. Make it clear to Kamalavathi that this burden of vengeance does not belong to King Uthama Purushan... My heartfelt blessings to the Maharaja’—that, Maharaja, is the message your father gave you... As soon as he asked me to tell you these final words, the Maharaja's life departed peacefully.

english_page_segments.english_text: ‘My grandson Ajayan himself must avenge the Pandiyan. Recovering my Navaratna throne is his responsibility.

Make it clear to Kamalavathi that this burden of vengeance does not belong to King Uthama Purushan... My heartfelt blessings to the Maharaja’—that, Maharaja, is the message your father gave you... As soon as he asked me to tell you these final words, the Maharaja's life departed peacefully.

notes: The source prints no speaker label on these continuation lines, so the English unit remains unlabelled despite the obvious dramatic continuity.

translation.english_text: Why are you crying, Amma!
No, my dear. Ajaya, that Pandiyan who killed your grandfather...
Give me the knife, Amma.....

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker continuation immediately after Ajayan asks for the knife.

translation.english_text: I'll cut off his head right now and bring it back.
notes: The source context strongly continues Ajayan, but no speaker label is printed and none is invented in metadata.

translation.english_text: Yes, there is no doubt about that, dear.

source_locator.description: Empty-speaker continuation after Kamalavathi's assurance to Ajayan.

translation.english_text: When you grow up, you will certainly do it...!
notes: No speaker label is manufactured for the source-empty field.

source_locator.description: Padmavathi, watching the play, places her hand on Manoharan beside her.

translation.english_text: (Watching the play, Padmavathi places her hand on Manoharan beside her.)
What is it, Amma...?
Nothing, my dear! The play...

source_locator.description: Source cue returning from the audience to the play.

translation.english_text: (In the play.)
Then I take my leave!
Varmare! You must remain in our palace itself as the chief court painter.
notes: The honorific address `வர்மரே` is kept as `Varmare` rather than flattened.

translation.english_text: My good fortune, Prabhu!
If your wife wishes, she may serve me as a maid.
Our good fortune, Mother!
(To herself) I am a maid; she, the Maharani who rules the realm! If tomorrow the times change...!
notes: The source-attached aside remains inside the immutable dialogue-linked unit.

source_locator.description: Vikatan is shown watching the play before an empty-speaker reaction line.

translation.english_text: (Vikatan is watching the play.)

source_locator.description: Reaction line following the Vikatan-watching direction; the printed speaker field is empty.

translation.english_text: Amma! Amma! She's quite something!...
notes: The preceding direction suggests Vikatan, but no speaker metadata is invented for the empty source field.

translation.english_text: Just like this, a court painter came to the palace... eighteen years ago...
His name?
Kesari Varman!

source_locator.description: Devasena dances to entrance Uthama Purushan; he gives her a pearl necklace.

translation.english_text: (In the play, Devasena dances to entrance King Uthama Purushan. The king gives her a pearl necklace as a gift.)

source_locator.description: Short source cue immediately before Varman addresses Devasena.

translation.english_text: (To Devasena.)
I have happy news for you! On behalf of our country's Kala Mandiram, I must tour the whole southern region. It is the Maharaja's order!
notes: `கலாமந்திரம்` is retained as `Kala Mandiram` rather than replaced with a modern institutional name.

translation.english_text: That is happy news for me! Hmm! You rascal!
notes: The source itself code-switches to `ராஸ்கல்`; the English keeps `rascal` plainly.

translation.english_text: No need to be in such a hurry... I am going to take you along too......
Is it true, Athaan?...... Only now are you my precious Athaan!... Ah!... I have passed all this time like a caged parrot... Athaan—here... I will ask the Maharani's permission and come right back.
notes: `Athaan` is retained to preserve Devasena's intimate register; the caged-parrot image is kept intact.

source_locator.description: Devasena falls down as she speaks.

translation.english_text: (As she says this, she falls down.)
Amma!... Amma!...... Wouldn't listen when told!......
Sena!
Has she fainted again?......
Then, before this too?......
What, master... do not speak as though you do not know. Amma!... in another nine months she is going to become a mother.
Ah... Sena is pregnant.
Then whose son is Vasanthan?
notes: The audience interjection is preserved as the source's pointed parallel between play and reality.

translation.english_text: Watch the play!
A play? Or what actually happened?
notes: The wordplay contrasts `நாடகம்` with `நடந்ததா`; the English retains the challenge rather than reducing it to a simple question.

source_locator.description: The next scene of the play states that Uthama Purushan and Devasena sing the love song identified by the printed words `நிலாவிலே ! சல்லாபமே!!`.

translation.english_text: As the next scene of the play, King Uthama Purushan and Devasena sing a love song — ‘In the Moonlight! Amorous Delight!!’
notes: Only the source-visible title/refrain reference is translated; no absent lyric body is supplied.
The unit is linked to `manohara-song-002`, whose authorship remains unresolved.

translation.english_text: Hmm... it seems the city inspection did not finish early today........
Yes... yes... it has indeed grown late... an unexpected amusement on the way......

Your words are amusing too... Perhaps even my staying awake here is an unexpected amusement to you... Swami...... Are these fashionable clothes for a city inspection?... Fine fragrance!... a box of javvadhu!... Oh!... You look as though you have only now returned from the bridal chamber... Who is your new bride, Swami?...
notes: The accumulating sarcastic questions and the source-specific `javvadhu` fragrance reference are retained.

translation.english_text: Curb your tongue when you speak... go, then—
Has your tongue become this foul? That Chandali's company.
notes: `சண்டாளி` is retained as the caste-marked insult `Chandali` rather than softened into a generic insult.

source_locator.description: The king slaps Kamalavathi on the cheek.

translation.english_text: (The king slaps Kamalavathi on the cheek.)

Maharaja! You have spoken arbitrarily, outside all reason and argument, and struck and hurt me without cause. I am not prepared to see you again; my eyes shrink even at the sight of you. Until the heat of your passion for the harlot Devasena subsides and you come of your own accord to see me, I will not come to see you—remember that well. Maharani Kamalavathi may not possess the beauty of your new Rati-devi. But a day will surely come in your life when you understand that this yellow marriage-thread of hers has a unique sanctity. Go then, to your holy service! Go.
notes: The speech's formal argumentative opening, insult, marital-symbol image and final sarcasm are preserved without compression.
`Rati-devi` and the yellow marriage-thread image are retained because generic wording would flatten the source's register and symbolism.

translation.english_text: You need not tell me! I am already going.

source_locator.description: Source cue `தேவசேனா தோழியிடம்.` before the poison instruction.

translation.english_text: Devasena, to her maid.
This dot is the mark... put the poison in this one. Careful......
Maharaja! I cannot remain here any longer... my heart is boiling.
Athaan... hot milk... the headache will fly away......
Sena, they say women of evil karma mix poison into milk even for their own husbands. Have you heard of that?
notes: The unusual source phrase `கர்மக் கள்ளிகள்` is rendered as `women of evil karma` rather than neutralized.

translation.english_text: No, Athaan... but there is nothing like that in this milk.
When you say so, what have I to fear? Sena, come here...... It has been a long time since I gave you milk with my own hand, hasn't it?........
Yes... all that was in the early days of marriage...
Chi... do not say that... drink...
It is like divine nectar, Athaan!......
All right... give it here. I will drink it myself.
Why... I will give it to you... hmm...
No! No! Poison!
notes: The source-visible audience interruption remains linked to its exact labelled dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Ha ha ha... the poison seems to be working... So this is the way of the clever......
notes: The taunting laugh and ironic `புத்திசாலிகள்` are retained.

translation.english_text: You... Rakshasi!... As though committing adultery were not enough, you poison your own husband to death too? Ah.........
notes: `Rakshasi` is retained as the source's mythic insult rather than softened.

translation.english_text: Are the sufferings I endured because of you one or two? You separated me from Rudrasenan, the love of my life! Now what I carry has flowered, set fruit and is ripening... If I kept you alive, would you not cut away something else too? That is why I got ahead of you... Who can stop your fate? Every fool who does not know how to understand his wife's mind meets this same fate, in every age......
notes: The flower/fruit/ripening metaphor is preserved without over-specifying what the source leaves figurative.
The final generalization about husbands is retained as Devasena's theatrical moral rather than softened.

source_locator.description: Varman dies; Vasantha Sena, watching the play, cries out for it to be stopped.

translation.english_text: Varman dies; Vasantha Sena, watching the play, cries out for them to stop it!

source_locator.description: Source cue immediately before the final unlabelled accusation voice.

translation.english_text: (A voice is heard.)

source_locator.description: Final accusation printed without a speaker label; spans PDF 18→19.

translation.english_text: She killed her husband! Rolled him into the forest torrent... Murderess! She is still alive! She is still alive.

english_page_segments.english_text: She killed her husband! Rolled him into the forest torrent...
Murderess! She is still alive! She is still alive.

notes: The repeated final accusation and its empty speaker field are preserved; no identity is assigned in metadata.
